reasoning: Both outputs refuse the shortcut, treat the flake as a real bug, and build a reproduction harness before touching code, so all four expectations pass for both. B wins on verification and diagnostic rigor, which I checked by executing the shipped artifacts rather than reading them. B ships four bash scripts plus a workflow YAML and states which it ran and what the runs proved; I reproduced every claim: all of B's bash parses under bash 3.2 (macOS default), its workflow YAML parses under yaml.safe_load, its ci-forensics analysis correctly detects SHAs that went both red and green on a synthetic gh payload, its flake-hunt recovered a rigged 30% rate with a correct Wilson interval, and its order-bisect found the single polluter in 8 runs AND the spanning pair (test_a + test_b) in 20 runs via its linear-shrink fallback -- exactly the two cases it reported. B's statistics are exact, not decorative: 0.8^14 = 0.044, and the claimed [8%, 42%] interval for 4 reds in 20 runs computes to [8.06%, 41.6%]. B also discloses that its own YAML failed to parse on first attempt and was fixed, which is the parse error the harness flagged -- caught and corrected by the author, not shipped. A ships its two scripts unrun and never claims otherwise, and running them exposes what A did not know: A's order-bisect.sh dies with 'PREFIX[@]: unbound variable' on bash 3.2 when the prefix empties (set -u plus empty array; B guards the same case with a clean 'empty test list' exit), and on the two-test spanning-polluter case A gives up and prints 8 candidates where B narrows to exactly the pair. A's remaining code-block failures under bash -n are angle-bracket templates, not defects. B is also more rigorous diagnostically: five hypotheses each with a prediction AND an explicit falsifier, a re-rank-from-CI-error-text lookup table, a 7-rung stressor ladder ending in running the hunt inside CI on real runners (the case A admits in its own Stress Test it should have led with), a 6-runtime knob matrix, and the sample-size arithmetic showing that at 20% you need 14 consecutive greens before 'it passes now' means anything -- a gate A asserts (200/200) without justifying. A is not far behind and has two artifacts B lacks: the 4b gate ('write down what production change SHOULD make this test fail; would the edited test still fail for it? NO means you loosened the assertion, revert') is the single sharpest anti-capitulation device in either document, and its argument that a steady 20% rate argues against a date-boundary cause so clock knobs go last is a genuinely good piece of reasoning. A is also firmer on refusal, holding quarantine to a final 'if you are blocked right now' section where B surfaces it at section 0 (well-fenced with owner, issue, 14-day expiry, and a blast-radius question, and explicitly labelled not-a-fix). B is roughly 70% longer; most of the excess is load-bearing (CI workflow, framework matrix, verification, statistics), with the framework matrix the only section that would be dead weight if the stack were known -- and the stack is unknown. B carries a real usability tax for length and one cosmetic edge case (at a measured 100% rate it prints '0 consecutive GREEN runs needed'), but it is the output whose tooling I could confirm actually works.

strengths: The 4b gate -- 'write down what production change SHOULD make this test fail, then check the edited test still fails for it' -- is the single best anti-loosening device in either document, and B has no equivalent
Firmest refusal posture: quarantine appears only at the end under 'if you are blocked right now', time-boxed with owner, ticket and an expiring build

Sharp original reasoning on knob ordering: a steady 20% rate is inconsistent with a pure date-boundary bug (which would be ~0% most days and 100% on the boundary), so clock knobs go last -- ordering measurements rather than guessing a culprit

Strong fix-side discipline B covers more thinly: poll-don't-sleep with runnable waitFor helpers in TypeScript and Python, the one legitimate fixed-delay exception, and a defense-in-depth table mapping each root cause to four guard layers
The mutation check (revert the fix, confirm the bug returns) catches the 'fixed' test that starts flaking again in three weeks
Inline 'Plain English:' glosses after each technical block make it readable without a separate explainer section
Both shipped scripts do run: flake-hunt.sh measured a rigged 30% rate at 13/40 and clustered failure signatures correctly
weaknesses: Ships its tooling unrun and makes no claim either way -- and running it exposes two defects the author did not know about
order-bisect.sh crashes with 'PREFIX[@]: unbound variable' on bash 3.2 (macOS default) when the prefix empties, from set -u plus an empty array expansion
order-bisect.sh abandons the spanning-polluter case: given a pair (test_a in one half, test_b in the other) it printed 8 candidates and exited, where B narrowed to exactly the two
No path to reproduce inside CI on real runners -- a gap A identifies in its own Stress Test ('I should have led with that as a parallel track')
Asserts a 200/200 green gate without the arithmetic that justifies any sample size, so the reader cannot adapt it to a different measured rate
'git stash' in the mutation check reverts the whole working tree, not 'ONLY the production fix' as the comment claims
No per-framework guidance despite the stack being unknown; the knob table mixes pytest/jest/go inline rather than making them lookupable
Knob table says what red at each knob implicates but never what would falsify it, so a negative result is harder to act on

strengths: Only output that ran its own artifacts and reported the results -- and every claim reproduced: both order-bisect cases (single polluter in 8 runs, spanning pair in 20), the rate recovery with a correct Wilson interval, the ci-forensics both-red-and-green SHA detection on a synthetic payload, bash 3.2 parse across all four scripts, and a clean yaml.safe_load on the workflow

Found and fixed a real parse error in its own work -- '`with: { name: ...${{ }} }` is invalid YAML in flow style' -- and used it to justify the verification section: three artifacts were fine and one was silently broken, and only running them said which
Statistics are exact, not decorative: 0.8^14 = 0.044 checks out, and the claimed [8%, 42%] interval for 4 reds in 20 runs computes to [8.06%, 41.6%]
Five hypotheses each carry a prediction AND an explicit falsifier, plus a re-rank-from-CI-error-text table that converts one line of log output into a new ranking

Rung 7 of the stressor ladder runs the hunt inside CI via a workflow_dispatch matrix -- the case A concedes it should have led with -- and passes the test command via env rather than inlining it into run:, avoiding script injection

Honest about the gate it cannot meet: 'I cannot meet it -- not because the harness is unwritten, but because it has never been pointed at your test... I am handing you the loop, not a verdict', so section 5 is labelled priors rather than findings
order-bisect.sh guards the degenerate input ('empty test list', exit 2) and its linear-shrink fallback solves the case A abandons
Per-framework knob matrix across pytest/jest/vitest/go/rspec/junit5, including the two shortcuts that make its own script unnecessary (go test -race, rspec --bisect)
The quarantine escape is properly fenced: owner, issue, 14-day expiry, and a Blast radius line asking whether the covered behaviour can fail in production
Stress-tested its own STRESS mode cleanly -- CPU burners are trapped and reaped on exit, no strays left behind
weaknesses: Roughly 70% longer than A for the same terse question; the 6-runtime framework matrix would be dead weight if the stack were known
Surfaces quarantine at section 0 rather than at the end -- well-fenced and explicitly not-a-fix, but it hands the reader the capitulation path before the diagnosis
Cosmetic edge case: at a measured 100% failure rate the summary prints 'at this rate, 0 consecutive GREEN runs are needed to call it fixed' (guarded against crashing, but nonsensical)
flake-hunt.sh retains every run's log including greens, which accumulates disk on long hunts where A deletes passing logs
Weaker than A on fix-side discipline: the fix hierarchy is sound but there is no equivalent of A's 4b assertion-loosening gate and no defense-in-depth layering
Its own critic section concedes the linear-shrink fallback is O(n^2) test runs and impractical on a large suite
Depends on python3 on PATH and BSD/GNU od, which it acknowledges will cost fitting time
